extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency policymakers, judges, and legal practitioners concerned with rulemaking and adjudication
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate agency practice and decisions against rule-of-law values (notice, justification, coherence, procedural fairness) in administrative rulemaking and adjudication. Focuses on how agencies should choose procedures, provide guidance, give reasons, and structure adjudications to satisfy legal and democratic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of choice of procedural form
rubrics_metrics.description: An obligation that the agency justify its choice of procedural form (e.g., adjudication versus rulemaking) rather than simply constraining agency choice; the agency should make a comparative assessment of available policymaking forms and explain why it selected one over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a minimal demand that could be specified as an obligation to explain why adjudication rather than rulemaking was used (for example, because the agency lacks information about how a statute impacts the regulated community or because of timing). The requirement bridges internal agency silos, forces deliberate decisionmaking in light of the agency’s full powers, and is analogous to procedural reporting requirements such as the Regulatory Flexibility Act’s regulatory flexibility analysis. While such a requirement risks judicial second‑guessing, it is positioned as a modest means of enforcing rule‑of‑law notice values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to issue guidance documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have a prima facie obligation to publish guidance documents that provide the public and regulated parties with the agency’s best statement of how it will apply statutory and regulatory sources, particularly when notice‑and‑comment rulemaking is impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published guidance promotes clarity, consistency, and publicity, creating internal ‘publication rules’ that bind lower‑level officials in practice even if not binding law. Guidance documents educate the public about agency intentions and create efficiencies for regulated parties. Definitions (e.g., Exec. Order No. 13,422) treat guidance as agency statements of general applicability and future effect that set policy or interpret statutes/regulations. Recent case law (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n) removed a doctrinal barrier to agencies altering guidance only through notice‑and‑comment, clearing the way for agencies to issue and revise guidance to comply with this obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and updating of guidance to ensure clarity and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance should be publicly published and periodically reevaluated and updated so it reflects the agency’s best understanding of the statutory scheme and provides predictable instruction to staff and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication channels agency discretion, reduces inconsistent application by lower‑level staff, and structures internal law. Agencies should treat guidance as prospective statements to be revised when the agency’s understanding changes; doctrinal changes allowing easier revision (Perez) facilitate this. Criticisms about back‑door regulation warrant careful drafting to ensure guidance remains non‑binding in form while providing meaningful direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned elaboration / requirement to give reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency action must be supported by reasoned elaboration: agencies must state reasons for their decisions across rulemaking (§553(c)), formal adjudication (§557), and other administrative actions (§555(e)), and courts generally uphold agency action only on the grounds the agency articulated at the time of decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason‑giving is foundational to administrative law and to judicial review under the arbitrary‑and‑capricious standard (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A)). The APA’s concise‑statement requirements impose procedural duties to explain basis and purpose. Agencies must avoid relying on post hoc justifications; reasoned explanation both guards against arbitrariness and is the currency by which agencies obtain judicial deference. Reason‑giving duties are especially demanding for agencies relative to other government actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification must be the product of participation (participatory justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency’s justification should be the culmination of a participatory process—i.e., reasons should reflect and respond to public participation—so that justification is not merely an official’s ex post rationalization but arises from a process that allowed stakeholders to present positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring that justifications be informed by participation raises tradeoffs: judicial enforcement of participation can incentivize well‑documented and well‑reasoned decisions but may also encourage pre‑proposal vetting with select stakeholders (diminishing meaningful public engagement). Effective design of review and participation incentives is necessary to combine rigorous documentation with genuine public input; courts’ ‘hard look’ review can empower those within agencies who favor reasoned elaboration but risks distorting the public comment process if agencies anticipate judicial requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of systemic coherence in statutory implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have a duty to implement statutory schemes so that legal norms fit together coherently: they must synthesize statutory text, past agency commitments, current policy preferences, and relevant background and constitutional norms to make the statutory regime intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because U.S. statutes are often ad hoc and lack integrated code‑like structure, the responsibility for systemic coherence falls heavily on agencies (and courts). Agencies should employ integrative statutory interpretation (Hart & Sacks style), mediate between past practices and present politics, and expose how changes fit into the statutory regime. Coherence is enforced in part through arbitrary‑and‑capricious review and should be assessed from the perspective of the regulated individual or firm so the law is intelligible and anchored in social expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of coherence obligations (locus and breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for coherence extends beyond narrow statutory exegesis to a broader obligation to read statutes in light of constitutional and background legal values; agencies are institutionally competent to incorporate these broader norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars defend agencies’ capacity to consider constitutional implications and background norms when interpreting statutes. Agencies’ statutory interpretation techniques should include integrating statutory obligations with constitutional commitments and other background values. Different specifications of coherence exist (textual emphasis versus policy/contextual emphasis), but agencies must make their implementation comprehensible within the legal system as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness: impartial decider and separation of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative adjudication requires an impartial decisionmaker; personnel who investigate or prosecute should not also decide, ensuring separation of enforcement staff from adjudicative decisionmakers to protect fairness and the appearance of neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA codifies separation principles (5 U.S.C. §554(d)): employees engaged in adversarial investigation or prosecution may not participate in decisions except as witness or counsel; hearing officers may not consult persons on facts in issue without notice and opportunity for parties to participate. However, APA protections do not fully extend to agency heads who may hear appeals; structural design must seek separation of personnel to preserve impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural protections for adjudicators (removal protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal protections (good‑cause protections) for adjudicators are a rule‑of‑law element because they protect the impartiality of adjudication by insulating decisionmakers from removal based on the merits of their decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court decisions (Humphrey’s Executor, Wiener) have supported removal protections where quasi‑judicial functions require insulation from political control; ALJs today commonly enjoy good‑cause protection (e.g., 5 U.S.C. §7521, Merit Systems Protection Board removal standards). While some recent cases may narrow the principle, removal protections remain an important structural guarantee of impartial adjudication and a core demand of procedural fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate rule‑of‑law compliance from regulated parties’ perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of agencies’ coherence and notice obligations should be made from the standpoint of the individual or firm subject to the law so that legal requirements are intelligible and expectations are anchored in social and political judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This perspective requirement helps ensure that agency explanations, guidance, and statutory implementations are not merely internally coherent but also produce understandable obligations for regulated entities; it supports integrating constitutional and background values into statutory implementation and grounds coherence in practical understandability.
